lead: Autocorrelation compares a random signal with a delayed copy of itself. Cross-correlation compares two different signals at different lags. The Fourier transform of the autocorrelation gives the power spectral density (PSD), which shows how power is spread over frequency; the transform of the cross-correlation gives the cross-PSD. Engineers use these tools to find hidden periods in sensor data, to detect a radar echo, to tune filters, and to describe noise in a communication link. The ideas need only wide-sense stationarity: a constant mean and an autocorrelation that depends on the lag alone.
prereq: You need: 7.2 Stationary processes for wide-sense stationarity, and Unit 4, Covariance.

blocks.text: A wide-sense stationary (WSS) process X(t) has a constant mean μ<sub>X</sub> and an autocorrelation that depends only on the time lag τ. The autocorrelation is R<sub>X</sub>(τ)=E[X(t)X(t+τ)]. Here E[·] is expectation, t is any time, and τ is the shift in seconds. R<sub>X</sub>(τ) measures how strongly a sample at time t resembles a sample τ seconds later.

At τ=0, R<sub>X</sub>(0)=E[X²(t)]. This is the mean-square value, also called the total average power of the process. If X(t) is a voltage in volts, R<sub>X</sub>(τ) has units of volts squared. The autocovariance removes the mean: C<sub>X</sub>(τ)=R<sub>X</sub>(τ)−μ<sub>X</sub>². At τ=0 it gives the variance σ<sub>X</sub>²=C<sub>X</sub>(0). When μ<sub>X</sub>=0, autocorrelation and autocovariance are the same.

blocks.where: R<sub>X</sub>(τ) is the autocorrelation; C<sub>X</sub>(τ) is the autocovariance; μ<sub>X</sub>=E[X(t)] is the constant mean; τ is the time lag.

blocks.text: Three properties are useful in exams. First, R<sub>X</sub>(−τ)=R<sub>X</sub>(τ): autocorrelation is even for a real process. Second, |R<sub>X</sub>(τ)|≤R<sub>X</sub>(0): the peak is at zero lag. Third, a periodic component in X(t) leaves a periodic ripple in R<sub>X</sub>(τ), which is how period detection works.

For two WSS processes X(t) and Y(t), the cross-correlation is R<sub>XY</sub>(τ)=E[X(t)Y(t+τ)]. It measures how much X at time t looks like Y, τ seconds later. The order matters: R<sub>YX</sub>(τ)=R<sub>XY</sub>(−τ). Cross-correlation is not even in general. The cross-covariance is C<sub>XY</sub>(τ)=R<sub>XY</sub>(τ)−μ<sub>X</sub>μ<sub>Y</sub>.
The power spectral density (PSD) shows how the average power of X(t) is distributed over frequency. The Wiener–Khinchin theorem says the PSD is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation.

blocks.where: S<sub>X</sub>(ω) is the power spectral density; ω is angular frequency in rad/s; j is the imaginary unit; the integrals run over all real values.

blocks.text: For a real process, S<sub>X</sub>(ω) is real, even, and non-negative: S<sub>X</sub>(ω)≥0 for every ω. A computed PSD that goes negative signals an algebra error.

Total average power is recovered by integrating the PSD: R<sub>X</sub>(0)=(1/2π)∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> S<sub>X</sub>(ω)dω. The factor 1/(2π) appears because the transform is in ω, not in ordinary frequency f=ω/(2π). For two processes, the cross-PSD is S<sub>XY</sub>(ω)=∫R<sub>XY</sub>(τ)e<sup>−jωτ</sup>dτ. It is complex in general.

sections.h3: Autocorrelation matrix for a random vector

blocks.text: For a random vector X=[X<sub>1</sub>,...,X<sub>n</sub>]<sup>T</sup>, the autocorrelation matrix R<sub>X</sub> is an n×n matrix with entries (R<sub>X</sub>)<sub>ij</sub>=E[X<sub>i</sub>X<sub>j</sub>]. Its diagonal entry (R<sub>X</sub>)<sub>ii</sub>=E[X<sub>i</sub>²] is a mean-square value, not a variance unless E[X<sub>i</sub>]=0.

The matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite. For any real vector a, a<sup>T</sup>R<sub>X</sub>a=E[(a<sup>T</sup>X)²]≥0. The autocovariance matrix is C<sub>X</sub>=R<sub>X</sub>−μμ<sup>T</sup>, where μ=E[X] is the mean vector. These matrices appear in array processing, beamforming, and principal component analysis.

figure.caption: The PSD S(ω)=16/(4+ω²) peaks at ω=0 with value 4 and is even about zero; at ω=±2 it is half the peak.

spec.aria: A symmetric power spectral density curve peaks at zero frequency and falls off as frequency increases.

examples.question: A zero-mean WSS process X(t) has autocorrelation R<sub>X</sub>(τ)=4e<sup>−2|τ|</sup>, with τ in seconds. Find the variance, the total average power, and the power spectral density S<sub>X</sub>(ω).
steps: The mean is μ<sub>X</sub>=0. The variance is C<sub>X</sub>(0)=R<sub>X</sub>(0)−μ<sub>X</sub>².
R<sub>X</sub>(0)=4e<sup>0</sup>=4. Thus variance = 4−0 = 4 (power units; volts squared if X is a voltage).
Use the standard transform ∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup>e<sup>−a|τ|</sup>e<sup>−jωτ</sup>dτ=2a/(a²+ω²) for a>0.
examples.answer: Variance = 4, total average power = 4, and S<sub>X</sub>(ω)=16/(4+ω²) (power units per rad/s).
examples.check:
A = 4.0
a = 2.0
variance = A
power = A
numerator = A * 2 * a
denominator_constant = a * a
print(variance)
print(power)
print(numerator)
print(denominator_constant)

traps: R<sub>X</sub>(0) is total average power, not variance unless μ<sub>X</sub>=0. For variance, use C<sub>X</sub>(0)=R<sub>X</sub>(0)−μ<sub>X</sub>².
The PSD transform is over the lag τ, not over t. Writing ∫R<sub>X</sub>(t)e<sup>−jωt</sup>dt confuses the time index with the lag.
R<sub>XY</sub>(τ) is not even in general. Check the order: R<sub>YX</sub>(τ)=R<sub>XY</sub>(−τ). Reversing the signals changes the sign of the lag.
The inverse formula needs 1/(2π) when ω is in rad/s. Dropping it makes the total power too large by 2π.
The diagonal of R<sub>X</sub> is E[X<sub>i</sub>²], not Var(X<sub>i</sub>), unless the mean is zero.

quiz.q: Define the autocorrelation R<sub>X</sub>(τ) of a WSS process X(t).
quiz.a: R<sub>X</sub>(τ)=E[X(t)X(t+τ)]: the expected product of the process at time t and at time t+τ.

quiz.q: Why is R<sub>X</sub>(0) called the total average power?
quiz.a: Because R<sub>X</sub>(0)=E[X²(t)], the mean-square value. For a voltage across 1 Ω, mean-square value is average power.

quiz.q: A zero-mean WSS process has R<sub>X</sub>(τ)=9e<sup>−3|τ|</sup>. Find the variance and S<sub>X</sub>(ω).
quiz.a: Variance = R<sub>X</sub>(0)=9. Use 2a/(a²+ω²) with a=3: S<sub>X</sub>(ω)=9·6/(9+ω²)=54/(9+ω²).

quiz.q: If μ<sub>X</sub>=2 and R<sub>X</sub>(0)=13, find the variance.
State the Wiener–Khinchin theorem in one sentence.
quiz.a: The power spectral density is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation function.

quiz.q: For WSS X and Y, R<sub>XY</sub>(τ)=0 for all τ. What does this imply?
quiz.a: X(t) and Y(t+τ) are orthogonal at every lag τ. They are uncorrelated at every lag only if μ<sub>X</sub>μ<sub>Y</sub>=0, that is, if at least one process has zero mean. It does not imply independence in either case.

quiz.q: A real WSS process has real even R<sub>X</sub>(τ). Show S<sub>X</sub>(ω) is even.
quiz.a: S<sub>X</sub>(−ω)=∫R<sub>X</sub>(τ)e<sup>jωτ</sup>dτ. Substitute u=−τ and use R<sub>X</sub>(−u)=R<sub>X</sub>(u); the integral equals S<sub>X</sub>(ω).

beyond: Not for the exam. Radar and sonar use cross-correlation to pull a weak echo out of noise. Speech and EEG analysis use PSD estimates to compare healthy and abnormal patterns. MIMO wireless and array processing rely on the autocorrelation matrix for beamforming and direction finding. Search for Welch periodogram, Yule–Walker equations, and spectral estimation if you want the practical next step.
